title: Lesotho achieves 98-99-99 HIV targets despite high prevalence in 2026 | HealthCare Middle East & Africa - No.1 Health & Pharma Manufacturing Industry Publication
summary: An estimated 256,400 people were living with HIV in Lesotho in 2025.

contentHtml:
LESOTHO—Lesotho has achieved the global 95-95-95 HIV targets, recording 98-99-99, according to figures presented in Maseru during the launch of the country’s World AIDS Day 2026 commemorative activities.

Speaking at the launch, Maema Ramaema of the National AIDS Commission (NAC) said the country had made considerable progress in its HIV response since recording its first case in 1986.

An estimated 256,400 people were living with HIV in Lesotho in 2025.

Women aged 15 and above accounted for 156,900 cases, while men in the same age group represented 93,100.

Children aged between zero and 14 accounted for the remaining 6,400 cases.

The country recorded approximately 3,300 new infections in 2025, an 84% decline from 2010.

AIDS-related deaths also fell by 65% over the same period to 3,400.

HIV prevalence remains high across districts

Despite progress in treatment coverage, Lesotho continues to face a substantial HIV burden.

Its adult HIV prevalence among people aged 15 to 49 stood at 16.3% in 2025, placing it behind Eswatini, which recorded 22.4%.

South Africa and Botswana followed at 15.9% and 14.7%, respectively.

Within Lesotho, Mafeteng recorded the highest prevalence at 17.6%, followed by Maseru at 17.3% and Leribe at 17.1%.

Botha-Bothe had the lowest rate at 13.9%, followed by Mokhotlong at 14.1% and Qacha’s Nek at 14.2%.

Ramaema acknowledged that the country continued to face significant challenges despite its progress against international treatment benchmarks.

Meanwhile, NAC Acting Chief Executive Tiisetso Piet cautioned against interpreting the reported figures as a complete picture of the epidemic.

She explained that the statistics reflected people accessing healthcare services at health facilities and might not capture individuals who do not routinely visit clinics.

Sustaining HIV prevention and treatment services

Lesotho has expanded HIV testing, antiretroviral treatment, prevention and public awareness programmes over the past four decades.

The decline in new infections and AIDS-related deaths reflects progress in controlling the epidemic, although the high prevalence rate continues to place pressure on the country’s healthcare system.

Maintaining treatment coverage will require sustained investment in HIV testing, early diagnosis, antiretroviral medicines and long-term patient monitoring.

Reaching people who remain outside formal healthcare services will also be important in sustaining progress, particularly as the country addresses differences in HIV prevalence across its districts.
